title: TypeScript SDK: incremental AST typegen, resilient discriminator fallbacks, and Zod hydration DSL
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Background:
The TypeScript SDK needs a robust path from model output -> typed application object across both streaming and non-streaming responses. Existing codegen attempts (single-pass JSON schema -> types) fail in two common production scenarios: 1) streaming partial shapes where early tokens determine union branches, and 2) models that produce slightly malformed discriminators (typoed tags or missing tag).

Goal:
Build an incremental, AST-driven type generator and runtime helper set that:
- Produces stable TypeScript types and Zod schema artifacts via an incremental AST approach (ts-morph) to minimize churn during small schema edits.
- Provides a runtime "resilient discriminator" policy that can apply heuristics and fallback rules when discriminators are missing/ambiguous (pattern match on shape, prefer numeric/tag mapping, consult a pinned model-schema hint).
- Exposes a Zod "hydration DSL" (small runtime helpers) that can progressively validate partial streaming tokens, stitch KV cache / prefix results, and produce either streaming validated events or a final hydrated object.
- Maintains compatibility with existing json-schema outputs so customers using JSON Schema still work.

Success criteria / acceptance:
- Codegen runs incrementally on a projected catalog of 1200 model prompts in under 12s on CI worker compared to baseline ~40s (measured).
- Streaming path: demo app can accept a streaming Chat response, validate partial events using the hydration helpers, and emit typed partials without false positive type errors in >95% of sampled prompts (based on eval harness).
- Runtime fallback correctly recovers ambiguous discriminators for at least 3 common classes (missing tag, variant spelled differently, and overlapping fields) with a negligible performance overhead (<6% p99 latency increase for standard calls).
- Unit / integration tests added; e2e example in repo and a short tutorial in docs.

Technical approach:
1) Incremental AST typegen
- Use ts-morph to produce compact edits to generated type files instead of full replace; keep a small, stable header comment and regenerate only affected nodes. This reduces noise for downstream repos and ensures smaller PRs for model catalog changes.
- Generator inputs: structured output schema (json-schema), inline discriminator metadata (tag names, alternative aliases), and streaming shape hints (prefix tokens that indicate branch). The generator emits: .d.ts types, .zod.ts validators, and an auxiliary hints file (JSON) the runtime can consult.

2) Resilient discriminator runtime
- Implement a deterministic policy chain: exact tag -> alias map -> shape-based matcher (field signature) -> model-hint lookup -> fallback-to-first-variant (with telemetry event). Each step emits structured diagnostics to tracing/console to help debugging.
- Provide a developer-configurable policy object: allow customers to prioritize alias maps or disable shape matching if they need strict validation.

3) Zod Hydration DSL & streaming ergonomics
- Provide small runtime primitives: partialValidate(zodSchema, partialPayload) returns either {status: "ok", partial} or {status: "needs_more"} with helpful path diagnostics; streamValidator(zodSchema, tokenStream) returns AsyncIterable<ValidationEvent> where ValidationEvent is union of PartialValid/Final/RecoverableError.
- Ensure the primitives are tree-shakeable and very small (target <8KB gzipped added to SDK bundle when imported). Implementation uses Zod's safeParse and lightweight incremental merge helpers; avoid adding another large runtime dependency.

Tradeoffs and decisions considered:
- ts-morph vs template-based emit: ts-morph chosen to support minimal diffs and to allow AST transforms for alias normalization; downside is larger dev dependency and more complexity in the generator.
- Heuristic discriminator matching: provides developer ergonomics but increases the chance of silent misclassification. Mitigation: emit telemetry events and require opt-in for auto-correction in enterprise mode.
- Streaming validator complexity: adding progressive validation yields better UX for streaming apps but complicates error handling. We will provide two modes: permissive (emit partial typed events with warnings) and strict (throw on first schema mismatch).

Implementation plan & milestones:
- Week 1 (spike, 3d): Prototype ts-morph emitter for small sample schema set; verify incremental edits on generated files. Link: spike PR.
- Week 2 (4d): Implement resilient discriminator policy and unit tests for three canonical failure modes.
- Week 3 (4d): Implement Zod hydration DSL and streaming validator; add example app that shows streaming typed partials.
- Week 4 (3d): Integration tests, perf validation, telemetry instrumentation, docs & tutorial.

Rollout and docs:
- Feature gated behind flag `TS_SDK_RESILIENT_OUTPUT=1` initially; enable for internal staging only.
- Docs: short how-to in SDK docs with code snippets for streaming usage, policy config, and migration guide from current json-schema workflow.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the long-term storage format for the hints file? (JSON vs compact binary). Action: product to decide; default JSON for now.
- Should we add a small CLI to inspect model-schema hints and run local validations? (UX win). Action: consider in next cycle as adder.

Acceptance tests / QA:
- Add unit tests for discriminator matching and alias maps.
- Add integration test that runs the streaming validator against the eval harness used by Runtime team (sample 500 prompts).
- Add a perf CI job that runs generator incrementally and compares times versus baseline.

Outcomes & follow-ups: 
- If successful, extend generator to emit Go and Python friendly artefacts (follow-up ENG ticket to coordinate SDK polyglot outputs).
- If heuristic fallbacks cause customer confusion, add stricter opt-in and telemetry-driven rollback plan.
